title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 87–88
description: Curated collective nouns and container-content expressions with original teaching examples and Brazilian Portuguese translations.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: All teaching sections, figures, container illustrations, exercises and relevant answer-key entries checked for lexical targets, semantic accuracy and natural collocations.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is supplied for securely identified short terms. Some longer phrases have empty IPA rather than an uncertain transcription; regional pronunciation differences are not exhaustively represented.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Study-page and illustrated-exercise comparison, answer-key cross-check, editorial and pronunciation review, structural schema/ID/audio-target validation.
audit.limitations: No bundled recordings were included. Browser-based TTS, speech recognition, and actual VocabLab import/round-trip were not tested in this environment.

units.title: Unit 87 — Collective nouns
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 180–181 (PDF pages 181–182).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Collective nouns and natural word combinations
learningObjectives: Choose suitable collective nouns for groups of people, animals, landscapes and everyday objects.
Distinguish a group, a crowd and a gang, and choose flock, herd, shoal, swarm or pack for animals.
Use occupational collective nouns such as crew, cast, staff and public with context-sensitive agreement.
Use combinations such as a bunch of flowers, a stack of chairs, and exercise-based groups of questions or complaints.

sectionsChecked: B: Words associated with certain animals
C: People involved in the same job/activity
D: Physical features of landscapes and picture
E: Things in general and illustrations

items.example: Flock is a collective noun used for groups of birds or sheep.
items.note: A noun that refers to a group as a unit.

items.example: A small group of people gathered outside the library.
items.note: A neutral collective expression for several people; often smaller than a crowd.

items.example: A crowd of people cheered as the runners crossed the finish line.
items.note: Crowd usually suggests a relatively large number gathered together.

items.example: The police arrested a gang of thieves operating near the station.
items.note: Gang can suggest a criminal or threatening group.

items.example: A flock of sheep crossed the road in front of the car.
items.note: Flock is typical with sheep and birds.

items.example: A flock of birds flew across the evening sky.
items.note: Flock is a natural collective noun for many species of birds.

items.example: A herd of cows was grazing beside the river.
items.note: Herd commonly describes large land mammals.

items.pt: um grupo de cervos; uma manada de cervos
items.example: A herd of deer appeared at the edge of the forest.
items.note: Deer has the same form in the singular and plural.

items.example: The farmer moved a herd of goats to another field.
items.note: Herd can be used for goats as well as cattle or deer.

items.example: A shoal of fish moved together beneath the boat.
items.note: Shoal is a common British English term for a group of fish.

items.example: We watched a shoal of herring swimming close to the shore.
items.note: The name of the fish can remain singular after shoal of.

items.example: A swarm of insects gathered around the streetlight.
items.note: Swarm is especially common for flying insects.

items.example: A swarm of bees settled in the old tree.
items.note: A group of bees moving or gathering together.

items.example: A pack of wolves was spotted in the national park.
items.note: Pack is common for wolves, dogs and hyenas.

items.example: A pack of dogs ran down the narrow street.
items.note: Pack describes dogs acting or moving as a group.

items.example: We bought a pack of cards for the train journey.
items.note: Pack also describes a complete set of playing cards; deck is common in American English.

items.example: A team of reporters arrived shortly after the announcement.
items.note: Team refers to people working together; British English may use a singular or plural verb depending on viewpoint.

items.example: A team of rescue workers searched the damaged building.
items.note: Team emphasises people cooperating on one activity.

items.example: The rescue crew reached the damaged vessel before dawn.
items.note: Crew refers to workers on a ship, aircraft or ambulance; British English allows singular or plural agreement depending on context.

items.example: The theatre company is preparing a new production.
items.note: Here company means a group of performers, not a commercial business.

items.example: The cast rehearsed the final scene several times.
items.note: The performers in a play or film; a collective cast can take singular or plural agreement in British English.

items.pt: o público; a população em geral
items.example: The public deserves clear information about the decision.
items.note: Collectively refers to people in general; singular or plural verbs are possible in British English.

items.example: The staff are discussing the proposed changes.
items.note: Normally takes a plural verb in British English when referring to employees.

items.example: The teaching staff are on strike over working conditions.
items.note: Fixed expression for employees who stop working as a protest.

items.example: A cast of actors performed the comedy for local schools.
items.note: Cast specifically refers to performers, not characters in a book.

items.pt: uma equipe de profissionais de ambulância
items.example: A crew of ambulance workers helped the injured cyclist.
items.note: Crew can name the people staffing an ambulance; hospital staff are not usually called a crew.

items.pt: uma fileira de casas de campo
items.example: A row of cottages stood beside the village green.
items.note: Row suggests things arranged side by side in a line.

items.example: A clump of trees sheltered the picnic area from the wind.
items.note: Clump suggests a compact cluster of trees or plants.

items.example: A range of hills stretched across the horizon.
items.note: Range indicates connected hills or mountains.

items.example: A group of islands lies just off the northern coast.
items.note: Group is a general collective term for nearby islands.

items.example: A pair of birds built a nest beneath the roof.
items.note: Pair refers to two related or matching things or creatures.

items.example: I added a couple of strawberries to the yoghurt.
items.note: A couple of usually means two, sometimes roughly two in informal speech.

items.example: A pile of papers was waiting on my desk.
items.note: Pile refers to items placed on top of one another, often untidily.

items.example: There was a heap of clothes on the bedroom floor.
items.note: Heap often implies an untidy or irregular pile.

items.example: She brought a bunch of flowers to the celebration.
items.note: Bunch is common for flowers and some fruits.

items.example: He picked a bunch of grapes from the vine.
items.note: A natural expression for grapes growing together.

items.example: A stack of chairs was stored behind the stage.
items.note: Stack suggests orderly items arranged one on top of another.

items.example: She keeps a set of tools in the workshop.
items.note: Set describes items that belong together and are used as a collection.

items.pt: um jogo de copos; um conjunto de copos
items.example: They received a set of glasses as a wedding present.
items.note: Set refers to a collection of matching household objects.

items.example: A swarm of mosquitoes made it difficult to sit outside.
items.note: Swarm also works for mosquitoes and other flying insects.

items.pt: um grupo de jovens com comportamento ameaçador
items.example: A gang of youths was shouting outside the shop.
items.note: Gang can imply menace; use group for a neutral description.

items.example: A team of biologists is monitoring the lake.
items.note: Team identifies specialists working towards a common goal.

items.example: A clump of fir trees stood beyond the farmhouse.
items.note: A more specific tree type used in the exercise matching task.

items.pt: uma cordilheira; uma cadeia de montanhas
items.example: A range of mountains separates the two regions.
items.note: An extended chain of mountains; compare a range of hills.

items.example: Investigators traced the stolen goods to a gang of criminals.
items.note: Gang is especially frequent for organised crime.

items.example: A swarm of flies gathered near the rubbish bins.
items.note: Swarm is appropriate for many insects flying together.

items.pt: um monte de roupas de cama
items.example: A heap of bed linen lay beside the washing machine.
items.note: Bed linen includes sheets and pillowcases; heap suggests an untidy collection.

items.example: The announcement raised a host of questions about safety.
items.note: Host of means a large number; often used with questions or problems.

items.example: The company received a barrage of complaints after the outage.
items.note: Barrage suggests many complaints arriving intensely or continuously.

items.example: The debate turned into a string of accusations.
items.note: String of describes several similar things in succession.

items.example: The spokesperson gave a series of brief answers.
items.note: Series of describes a sequence; series is unchanged in the plural.

units.title: Unit 88 — Containers and contents
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 182–183 (PDF pages 183–184).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Recognise and pronounce common containers, including carton, jar, jug, packet, sack, tin, tub and tube.
Choose natural container-and-content collocations for food, drinks, household products and storage.
Describe packaging materials and distinguish packaging for single items, liquids and bulk goods.
Identify container expressions illustrated in the exercises and recognise British and American vocabulary differences.

sectionsChecked: B: Materials and typical contents table

items.example: She carried the shopping home in a reusable bag.
items.note: A flexible container made from cloth, paper or plastic.

items.example: The olive oil was stored in a large barrel.
items.note: A large rounded container traditionally made of wood and metal.

items.example: He put the freshly washed clothes into a basket.
items.note: An open container, often woven, for carrying or storing things.

items.example: Please put the empty bottle in the recycling bin.
items.note: A narrow-necked container, usually of glass or plastic.

items.example: She served the fruit in a large bowl.
items.note: An open, rounded container for food and other materials.

items.example: The documents were packed in a cardboard box.
items.note: Usually a rigid container, often rectangular.

items.example: He filled a bucket with water to clean the floor.
items.note: An open container with a handle, often used for liquids.

items.example: She opened a can of cola after lunch.
items.note: Typically a metal drinks container; in American English also common for canned food.

items.example: They keep a carton of milk in the fridge.
items.note: A carton is made of card or layered packaging material.

items.example: His spare glasses were kept in a protective case.
items.note: A container made to protect or carry particular objects.

items.example: A worker unloaded a crate of bottles from the van.
items.note: A sturdy container for transporting several items, often bottles.

items.example: He poured some water into a clean glass.
items.note: Countable for the drinking vessel; glass is also an uncountable material.

items.pt: pote de vidro; vidro com tampa
items.example: She washed the empty jam jar to use it again.
items.note: A rigid container, usually with a wide opening and a lid.

items.example: A jug of water stood in the middle of the table.
items.note: A handled vessel with a lip for pouring liquids; American English often says pitcher.

items.example: He drank his tea from a large mug.
items.note: A drinking vessel with a handle, usually for hot drinks.

items.example: She bought a pack of playing cards.
items.note: A group of items packaged or sold together.

items.example: He opened a packet of biscuits to share.
items.note: Typically a small wrapped or packaged quantity; British English.

items.example: The soup was warming in a pan on the stove.
items.note: A metal cooking vessel; its shape depends on the kind of pan.

items.example: She planted the herb in a small pot.
items.note: Often a small container for food, paint or a plant.

items.example: They carried the potatoes in a heavy sack.
items.note: A large, tough bag for bulky materials.

items.example: We bought a tin of tomatoes for the sauce.
items.note: British English commonly uses tin for a container of preserved food.

items.example: There was an empty ice-cream tub in the freezer.
items.note: A wide, open-topped container, commonly of plastic.

items.example: I packed a small tube of toothpaste for the trip.
items.note: A squeezable container for cream, paste or ointment.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: The children shared a bag of sweets after the game.
items.note: Bag is natural for a flexible package of small items.

items.pt: um barril de óleo; um barril de petróleo
items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: Workers rolled a barrel of oil into the storage area.
items.note: Barrel is commonly used for large quantities of liquid.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: A basket of clothes was waiting to be folded.
items.note: Basket is often an open container used for laundry.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: We took a bottle of lemonade on the picnic.
items.note: Bottle usually refers to glass or plastic packaging for drinks.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: A bowl of soup helped her warm up after the walk.
items.note: Use bowl for food served in a deep, open dish.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: He kept a box of matches in the kitchen drawer.
items.note: A conventional combination for matches.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: She used a bucket of water to rinse the floor.
items.note: Bucket commonly measures or holds water.

items.pt: uma lata de refrigerante de cola
items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: She put a can of cola in the picnic bag.
items.note: A metal drinks container; one can is one individual unit.

items.pt: uma caixinha de suco; uma embalagem de suco
items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: We bought a carton of juice for the journey.
items.note: Carton is a natural packaging unit for juice and milk.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: He bought a padded case for glasses.
items.note: Case protects an item; it is not normally a serving measure.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: The café ordered a crate of bottles for the weekend.
items.note: Crate is used for transporting or storing multiple bottles.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: Could you bring me a glass of water, please?
items.note: Glass of measures a serving of a drink.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: She opened a jar of honey for breakfast.
items.note: Jar is normally a rigid container with a lid.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: The waiter put a jug of milk beside the coffee.
items.note: Jug has a pouring spout and often a handle.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: He made a mug of coffee before starting work.
items.note: Mug is a common serving vessel for hot drinks.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: We found a pack of cards in the cupboard.
items.note: A pack of cards is a complete set used for card games.

items.pt: um pacote de batatas fritas tipo chips
items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: They shared a packet of crisps on the train.
items.note: Crisps is British English; American English usually says chips.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: There was a pan of food simmering on the stove.
items.note: Pan commonly refers to food being prepared on a cooker.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: I brought a pot of yoghurt for my afternoon snack.
items.note: A small pot is a common British English packaging unit for yoghurt.

items.pt: um saco grande de carvão mineral
items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: They delivered a sack of coal to the old house.
items.note: Sack is suitable for heavy, loose solids.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: He opened a tin of sardines for lunch.
items.note: British English uses tin; American English commonly uses can.

items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: We bought a large tub of ice cream for the party.
items.note: Tub is common for ice cream sold in a wide container.

items.pt: uma bisnaga de pasta de dente
items.section: B · Common container and content pairs
items.example: She put a tube of toothpaste in her travel bag.
items.note: Tube refers to flexible packaging squeezed to release its contents.

items.pt: um pote de pasta de amendoim
items.example: We opened a jar of peanut butter for breakfast.
items.note: The picture exercise shows peanut butter in a lidded jar.

items.pt: um pacote de sabão em pó
items.example: She picked up a packet of washing powder at the shop.
items.note: The illustration presents washing powder in a packet or box.

items.pt: uma caixinha de creme de leite
items.example: The recipe calls for a carton of cream.
items.note: Cream can be sold in a carton rather than a bottle.

items.pt: uma bisnaga de creme para as mãos
items.example: She keeps a tube of hand cream in her handbag.
items.note: Tube is commonly used for creams and ointments.

items.pt: uma lata de feijão em conserva
items.example: He heated a tin of beans for a quick meal.
items.note: Tin is British English for a can of preserved food.

items.pt: um saco de maçãs; uma sacola de maçãs
items.example: We brought home a bag of apples from the market.
items.note: Bag is suitable for a quantity of loose fruit.

items.pt: uma caixa de lenços de papel
items.example: There is a box of tissues beside the sofa.
items.note: Tissues are often dispensed from a cardboard box.

items.example: She took a packet of butter out of the fridge.
items.note: Butter may be sold in a wrapped packet or block.

items.example: They carried a pack of six cans into the kitchen.
items.note: Pack often means several items sold together.

items.pt: um frasco de detergente de louça
items.example: He bought a bottle of washing-up liquid for the kitchen.
items.note: Washing-up liquid is British English for dishwashing liquid.

items.example: She gave her neighbour a box of chocolates.
items.note: Typically a gift box of individual chocolates.

items.example: We shared a packet of biscuits during the break.
items.note: Biscuits is British English; American English often says cookies.

items.example: They brought a bottle of wine to dinner.
items.note: A common container-content collocation.

items.example: He opened a jar of jam for his toast.
items.note: Jam is normally sold in lidded jars.

items.example: A small bowl of sugar was placed beside the teapot.
items.note: Bowl can hold loose or granulated ingredients.

items.pt: uma caixa de garrafas de vinho
items.example: The restaurant ordered a case of wine for the event.
items.note: Case can refer to a shipping box holding several bottles.

items.pt: uma lata ou pote de tinta
items.example: She opened a pot of paint to repair the wall.
items.note: Pot may be used for a container of paint, especially a small one.

items.example: The pharmacist gave him a tube of ointment.
items.note: Ointment is often supplied in a squeezable tube.

items.example: He picked up a carton of milk from the shop.
items.note: Milk is often sold in cartons made from card and protective layers.

items.example: We ordered a bottle of milk with our groceries.
items.note: Milk can also be packaged in glass or plastic bottles.

items.example: They opened a tin of tuna for the salad.
items.note: A common British English quantity expression for preserved fish.

items.pt: um pacote de biscoitos de chocolate
items.example: He brought a packet of chocolate biscuits to share.
items.note: The exercise uses packet or box for packaged biscuits.

items.example: The farmer lifted a heavy sack of potatoes onto the truck.
items.note: The answer key gives sack as a container for bulk vegetables.

items.example: We opened a jar of olives to serve with lunch.
items.note: Olives are commonly sold in lidded glass jars.

items.example: She carried a box of tools to the workshop.
items.note: Box can contain tools as well as household items.
